source: Ko and Uttl (2003) Individual differences in program comprehension strategies in unfamiliar programming systems
finding: Three comprehension strategies were found by cluster analysis of logged actions in an unfamiliar language (Stata). They tracked programming experience. No strategy won on debugging. Bug-specific domain knowledge predicted success best.
numbers: 86 recruited, 75 analysed; 20-minute debugging task, 4 seeded bugs; over 33,000 coded actions; Ward clustering, 3 clusters; mean bugs fixed 1.00 (depth-first, info-seeking), 1.65 (inactive, spec-focused), 2.00 (breadth-first, experienced); clusters 2 and 3 judged comparable.
quote: The results presented here are largely inconsistent with studies on debugging in familiar programming systems
limits: Exploratory; one task and tool; mostly undergraduates; gender confounded with major; authors say the result is largely inconsistent with studies in familiar systems, where expert strategy beat novice strategy.
agent_relevance: Strategy label matters less than having the right domain knowledge for the specific fault. Give S1/S2 reading a step to pull in domain facts about the failing behavior, not a fixed read order.

source: Busjahn et al. (2015) Eye movements in code reading: relaxing the linear order
finding: Novices read code less linearly than prose. Experts read code even less linearly, skipping lines in a way closer to execution order than to top-to-bottom story order.
numbers: 14 novices (Java course, longitudinal) plus a group of professional experts (count not extracted); about 80% linear eye moves on natural text, 70% on code for novices, 60% on code for experts; novices looked directly at 52.42% of code elements vs 41.27% for experts (U=84, p<0.01); regression rate showed no difference (p=0.97).
quote: novices read source code less linearly than they read English text
limits: Small samples (novice paired tests had df 6); German-speaking participants; Java only; eye tracker mapped only 72.7% of expert fixations to lines.
agent_relevance: A human expert does not read code top to bottom. An agent that dumps a file in order is acting like a novice; reading should follow call and data paths.

source: Peitek, Siegmund and Apel (2020) What drives the reading order of programmers? An eye tracking study (non-exact replication of Busjahn 2015 and Peachock 2017)
finding: Partial replication. Experience effect on linearity replicated for vertical moves but not for the NW sequence score. Code linearity (jumps in execution order) had a stronger effect than experience. Comprehension strategy (top-down vs bottom-up) had a minor effect. Peachock's null on experience was contradicted.
numbers: 12 novices and 19 intermediate programmers; correctness 86% vs 91% (U=11121, p=0.072); mixed models with FDR-corrected alpha 0.033; novice vs intermediate: vertical next p=0.003, vertical later p=0.010, vertical regressions p=0.008, story-order NW score p=0.932; code linearity p=0.000 on all measures; strategy: vertical regressions BU>TD p=0.000, saccade length p=0.046 (not significant after FDR); no interaction effects.
limits: Intermediate not expert group; strategy forced by meaningful vs obfuscated identifiers, which manipulates cues rather than the reader's chosen strategy; short snippets (up to 30 lines).
agent_relevance: The reader's order is driven more by how non-linear the code is than by who reads. Code structure (jumps) should drive what the agent reads next.

source: Peachock et al. (2017) replication of Busjahn 2015 with C++ and a Tobii X60 (as reported in Peitek 2020)
finding: As summarised by Peitek et al.: replicated that code is read less linearly than text, and replicated the NW score difference between text and code. Did not replicate a novice-versus-expert linearity difference.
numbers: Eye tracker at 60 Hz; p-values for experience on vertical next 0.406, vertical later 0.461, vertical regressions 0.453, horizontal later 0.487 (from table in Peitek 2020).
limits: Read only through Peitek et al.; original not opened. C++ not Java; student participants.
agent_relevance: Shows the novice-expert reading-order gap is fragile; do not hard-code an expert reading order as a rule.

source: Siegmund et al. (2014) Understanding understanding source code with functional magnetic resonance imaging
finding: Bottom-up comprehension (obfuscated identifiers, compute the output) versus finding syntax errors activated five left-hemisphere regions tied to working memory, attention and language.
numbers: 17 participants in the scanner; areas BA 6, 21, 40, 44, 47; FDR p<0.01; on average 90% of participants got the output right.
limits: Small N; short snippets; bottom-up forced by removing beacons; fMRI tasks cannot be realistic; Brodmann mapping is coarse.
agent_relevance: Reading code without beacons loads working memory and language areas. Evidence that the cost of bottom-up reading is real and that names do work.

source: Wagner and Wyrich (2021) Code comprehension confounders: a study of intelligence and personality
finding: Fluid intelligence, visual perception and cognitive speed correlate weakly with comprehension correctness; crystallized intelligence and personality do not. The full model explains only about 10% of variance.
numbers: 135 undergraduates recruited (117 with complete data per the paper); two Java methods, 10 questions each; standardised beta (Holm-adjusted p): Gf 0.299 (.0078), Gv 0.261 (.027), Gs 0.247 (.034), Gc 0.188 (.138, ns), conscientiousness -0.096 (.54), openness -0.040 (.64); adjusted R2 = .096 for the full model, .122 after stepwise selection.
quote: personality traits are unlikely to impact code comprehension performance
limits: Correlational; authors call it underpowered; two snippets only; students; paper test.
agent_relevance: Comprehension tracks general reasoning ability a little, and about 90% of variance is elsewhere. Supports a scaffold that applies the same checks for every reader instead of relying on raw ability.

source: Langhout and Aniche (2021) Atoms of Confusion in Java (replication of Gopstein et al. for C)
finding: Replicated that confusing micro-patterns raise error rates, now in Java with novices. Seven of 14 atoms were significantly confusing in correctness; ten of 14 were rated more confusing side by side. Some C atoms did not replicate.
numbers: 132 CS students in a two-phase study (96 completed part of it); 115 wrong of 315 answers with atoms vs 46 wrong of 337 without; pooled odds ratio 3.82 (95% CI 2.69 to 5.42); per-atom OR from 2.70 (pre-increment) to 56.21 (conditional operator, CI 0.81 to 284); post-increment OR 12.95; perceived confusion disagreed with Gopstein for some atoms.
limits: Novices only; Java translation of C atoms; some wide CIs; online unsupervised task.
agent_relevance: Surface-level traps (increment order, implicit conversions) mislead readers. An agent that simulates code mentally should check such constructs by executing them.

source: Gopstein et al. (2017) Understanding misunderstandings in source code (original atoms-of-confusion study, as cited by Langhout and Aniche)
finding: Original C study: programmers make significantly more mistakes on code with atoms. Cited in the replication as involving 220 professional programmers.
numbers: No numbers re-checked here; the replication reports a table comparing atom by atom.
limits: Not opened; known only via the Java replication.
agent_relevance: Baseline claim for line b07.

source: Lavazza, Morasca and Gatto (2023) An empirical study on software understandability and its dependence on code characteristics
finding: Structural code measures (LOC, McCabe, Cognitive Complexity) predict understanding time poorly. Average prediction error about 30%. Cognitive Complexity gave no real gain.
numbers: 3 Master's students, 32 methods from 2 open-source Java projects; maintenance tasks (locate and fix a fault); all methods corrected; mean times per participant 27.2, 28.8, 28.9; machine-learning models with one or two measures; mean error about 30%.
limits: Only three participants; time as understandability proxy; fault-fixing task rather than pure comprehension.
agent_relevance: Complexity scores will not tell the agent which code is hard to read; use behavior (tests and traces) instead.

source: Lavazza, Abualkishik, Liu and Morasca (2022 preprint) An empirical evaluation of the Cognitive Complexity measure as a predictor of code understandability
finding: Reanalysed datasets from earlier studies (dataset ids 1 to 10). Cognitive Complexity correlated with understandability about as much as traditional measures. Models with it were not better than models without.
numbers: Support Vector Regression models; datasets cover time, ratings, correctness and physiological signals; CoCo never achieved the best result on correctness datasets.
limits: Secondary analysis of heterogeneous and small datasets; measures differ across studies.
agent_relevance: A claimed cognitive metric that fails to deliver is a warning against building the scaffold around a single complexity score.

source: Rong et al. (2026) Can perplexity serve as a cognitive signal for code understandability?
finding: Snippet-level LLM perplexity does not reliably track human understandability, even though token-level perplexity tracked local confusion. Human labels also lack consensus.
numbers: Largest absolute correlation 0.373 (consensus IQR diagnostic, p=0.233); P90 correlation rose from 0.115 to 0.235 after consensus filtering; most correlations small and not significant across method-level, output-prediction and patch datasets.
limits: Small human datasets; authors treat p-values as exploratory; depends on tokenizer and model.
agent_relevance: Do not use the model's own surprise as a gauge of how hard code is. It is a local alarm, not an overall difficulty score.

source: Abdelsalam et al. (2025) How do humans and LLMs process confusing code?
finding: Perplexity spikes of an LLM (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B) line up in place and size with human EEG fixation-related potentials on atoms of confusion. A perplexity-based detector found 64% of labelled atoms.
numbers: 24 human participants with 72 trials each (data from an earlier study); Spearman rho 0.37 (95% CI 0.19 to 0.53) in confusing snippets; rho 0.31 (CI 0.10 to 0.50) for a second aggregation; detector hit 64% of labelled atoms and flagged 85 new regions in confusing and 69 in clean snippets.
limits: One model; Java; human signals from an older study; moderate correlation; later work (b11) found it does not scale to snippet level.
agent_relevance: LLMs and humans stumble on similar tokens. Where the model is surprised at a token, treat that token as a candidate for a check by execution.

source: Haroon et al. (2026, ICST) Assessing the impact of code changes on the fault localizability of large language models
finding: LLM fault localisation is brittle to meaning-preserving edits and biased toward code seen early. Misleading names and comments hurt.
numbers: 10 LLMs, 750,013 fault-localisation tasks; 78% of previously correct localisations fail after semantic-preserving mutations; accuracy falls 1.04% per mutation step in Java and 1.93% in Python; 56% of correct localisations lie in the first 25% of lines vs 6% in the last 25%; function reordering gave an 83% accuracy drop.
limits: Injected faults, not real bugs; specification given; underspecified programs filtered out.
agent_relevance: The model reads like a shallow reader. Re-check with restated or reordered views before trust. Do not rely on position in context.

source: Abdollahi et al. (2025) Demystifying errors in LLM reasoning traces: code execution simulation
finding: Reasoning LLMs predict program output well on most inputs, yet make nine kinds of inference errors. A tool-augmented approach corrected 58% of computation errors.
numbers: 427 snippets from HumanEval+ and LiveCodeBench, 12 inputs each (regular, edge, invalid); four reasoning LLMs (DeepSeek-R1, o4-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude 4 Sonnet) at 85% to 98% accuracy; tool fix on 58% of computation errors; about 40% remain.
limits: Short competitive-programming style code; error taxonomy built by the authors.
agent_relevance: Mental execution is good but not enough. Use real execution for arithmetic and state, which fixes more than half of this error class.

source: Kou et al. (2024) Do large language models pay similar attention like human programmers when generating code?
finding: Model attention differs from where programmers look in the task description. Perturbation-based attention is closer to human and preferred in a user study. About 27% of generation errors fit five attention patterns.
numbers: 6 LLMs incl. GPT-4; 12 attention methods; human labels on 974 MBPP tasks (Cohen kappa 0.73, 192 person-hours); on average 7 of 29.6 words marked important; 211 wrong programs analysed; 27% explained by five patterns; user study 22 participants; 14 of 22 still lacked trust.
limits: Generation, not comprehension; description text not code; human attention was labelled, not eye-tracked.
agent_relevance: Where the model attends in the problem statement can be wrong. Restating key constraints explicitly early is a cheap correction.

source: Tang et al. (2024) Developer behaviors for validating and repairing LLM-generated code using eye tracking and IDE actions
finding: Developers validating Copilot code use similar strategies whether or not they are told the origin, but those not told often fail to spot it. Knowing provenance improved performance but raised workload and search effort.
numbers: 28 participants in 2 groups (informed vs not); eye tracking, IDE logs, NASA-TLX; almost 80% (11 of 14) of uninformed participants did not identify the code as LLM-made.
limits: Lab study; three projects; small groups; Copilot of 2023.
agent_relevance: Reviewing model-written code is a different reading task. Label each piece by origin in the scaffold so the reader switches to verification.

source: Richards and Wessel (2024) What you need is what you get: Theory of Mind for an LLM-based code understanding assistant
finding: A mind-modelling prompt (ToMMY) did not change novice quiz scores overall. The authors report a positive effect for bottom-up users and a negative one for top-down users; programming experience did predict scores.
numbers: 14 novices in a within-subject test, 28 sessions; ToMMY quiz coefficient 0.05 (p=0.61), time -28.94 s (p=0.50); programming experience 0.10 (p<0.01); 6 of 14 phrased hypotheses.
limits: Very small; subgroup split post hoc; link to Brooks model is by interpretation.
agent_relevance: An aid that helps a bottom-up reader may hurt a top-down one. Do not assume one reading aid fits all states.

source: Kaufman, Brun, Murali and Endres (2026) Programmers are poor and overconfident judges of LLM-generated assertions
finding: Humans judge correct assertions fairly (74%) but incorrect ones at chance (49%) with equal confidence. Natural-language explanations gave no net benefit; low-quality ones hurt accuracy and raised confidence. Think-aloud responses were coded as top-down, bottom-up or as-needed.
numbers: 86 Python programmers in a pre-registered controlled experiment; OR 2.94 for correct vs incorrect (p<0.001); poor explanation effect p=0.037; confidence 3.99 vs 4.25 out of 5; in the think-aloud follow-up, 7 responses bottom-up, 10 as-needed, 2 unclear, with participants primarily top-down overall (top-down count not extracted); intuition was wrong in 7 of 12 incorrect responses.
limits: HumanEval-style functions; one task type; think-aloud on a subset.
agent_relevance: Humans confirm what looks right. An agent verifying by reading shares this bias; verification should try to refute, with executed counter-examples.

source: Qiao, Shihab and Hundhausen (2025) Systematic review of GenAI assistants for code comprehension
finding: Across 31 studies from 2022 to 2024, assistants often give inaccurate or unclear explanations and novices struggle to write good prompts. The review restates that novices tend to bottom-up and experts to top-down.
numbers: 31 studies reviewed; no pooled effect size.
limits: Mostly small education studies; the novice/expert claim is restated from earlier literature, not tested.
agent_relevance: Reading help from the model needs checking by tests; do not treat explanations as ground truth.

source: Wyrich, Bogner and Wagner (2023) 40 years of designing code comprehension experiments: a systematic mapping study
finding: The field is methodologically uneven. Only one replication met inclusion criteria. Few between-subject designs balance groups by skill. Students dominate.
numbers: 95 experiments (1979 to 2019); median 34 participants (range 5 to 277); journals median 61, conferences 26, workshops 26; 53.7% all-student samples, 9.5% only professionals; 47% used Java; only 6 of 25 between-subject experiments balanced experience (24%); about one third of within-subject designs did not counterbalance; no study looked at consequences of comprehension on any other construct.
limits: Mapping study, not an effect-size meta-analysis; a 2026 corrigendum exists and was not opened.
agent_relevance: The human comprehension literature is thin and small-sample. Treat any single effect as provisional when choosing scaffold rules.

source: Munoz Baron, Wyrich, Graziotin and Wagner (2023) Evidence profiles for validity threats in program comprehension experiments
finding: Authors rarely back validity threats with evidence. For the three most cited threats, the cited evidence mostly failed the authors' criteria.
numbers: 31 of 409 threat mentions cited supporting evidence; for programming experience, program length and comprehension measure, 17 of 18 cited studies did not meet the evidence criteria.
limits: Systematic search plus thematic synthesis by the authors; criteria are theirs.
agent_relevance: Even the claim that experience moderates comprehension is not firmly backed. Keep the scaffold independent of such claims.

source: Feitelson (2021) Considerations and pitfalls in controlled experiments on code comprehension
finding: Method guide: subjects may find shortcuts, metrics measure different things, student-versus-professional is too crude, and obfuscating names changes strategy.
numbers: No new data. Notes that Siegmund et al. used obfuscated names to force bottom-up comprehension; time and correctness are separate metrics.
limits: Position paper; no effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Where a task lets the agent reach the answer by a shortcut (for example memorised benchmarks), it is not reading code at all.

source: Bexell et al. (2024, PPIG) How do developers approach their first bug in an unfamiliar code base?
finding: Five professionals use mixed strategies in large unfamiliar programs: reproduce, localise, simulate. They cite von Mayrhauser et al. that understanding of large code is by necessity partial.
numbers: 5 interviews; 2 to 27 years of experience; share of time on comprehension 58% (Xia 2018) to 70% (Minelli 2015) cited from earlier work.
limits: Tiny qualitative sample from one region and employer; interview self-report.
agent_relevance: For large repos, the as-needed pattern (reproduce first, localise, read only what matters) is the practitioner way. It argues for S1 to start from a failing run.

source: Chain of Understanding (2025) hierarchical LLM guide for code auditing (search listing only)
finding: Search listing says it proposes LLMs that guide developers through hierarchical comprehension from a high-level overview downward.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened; listing only.
agent_relevance: Possible tool for top-down S1 reading; unverified.

source: Brooks (1983), Letovsky (1986) and von Mayrhauser and Vans (1995) comprehension models (as described in Ko and Uttl, Peitek and Kaufman)
finding: Seen only through citations: top-down is hypothesis driven and uses domain knowledge; bottom-up builds control and data flow from code; the integrated model lets the reader switch; as-needed means looking things up when a question arises.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened; secondary description. No data here discriminates the models.
agent_relevance: Model background only. The collected data do not settle which model is right.

source: Lin and Robles (2023) Investigating the impact of vocabulary difficulty and code naturalness on program comprehension (registered report)
finding: Registered-report protocol only. Plans to test whether harder vocabulary and lower naturalness relate to readability and understandability; notes that earlier work found little correlation of metrics with understandability.
numbers: Kendall rank correlations planned on existing datasets; no results.
limits: No data in this document.
agent_relevance: No finding to use; shows the field still lacks predictors of comprehension.
